tldr: By optimizing and parallelizing a learning pipeline using world models and analytic gradients with JAX, humanoid motion tracking and rough-terrain locomotion can now be learned in under a minute.
hero_caption: Motions acquired by the Unitree G1 in less than a minute of training using four NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The top row shows XMimic tracking a dance motion from the LAFAN1 dataset after 54 seconds of training, and the bottom row shows XSoma walking stably on rough terrain while following velocity commands after 46 seconds of training.
overview:
Reinforcement learning for humanoid robots has accelerated dramatically from days to minutes with the advent of GPU-parallel simulation. In particular, methods like SuperMimic—which learn a "world model" to predict robot dynamics instead of learning directly inside a simulator, and then optimize policies via backpropagation (analytic gradients) through imagined trajectories—are known to offer exceptional sample efficiency and drastically cut computational cost. However, existing implementations suffer from long computational chains made of many small GPU operations strung together in serial. Because of these sequential dependencies, scaling up to larger GPUs could not parallelize the computation, causing wall-clock time to hit a plateau. Furthermore, for tasks like rough-terrain locomotion, model-free reinforcement learning still remained overwhelmingly faster.

To overcome these hurdles, the authors propose "XMimic" and "XSoma," introducing radical shortening of the computational chain alongside smart pipeline distribution across multiple GPUs. The entire training loop, including the simulator (MuJoCo Warp/MJX), is compiled end-to-end with JAX, eliminating idle waiting between steps. For motion tracking, XMimic uses pipeline parallelism by assigning data collection, world model updates, and policy updates to different GPUs. For rough-terrain locomotion, XSoma adopts a parallel approach that computes successive policy gradients simultaneously across different GPUs. For locomotion, only the robot's joint dynamics are left to the world model, while values like terrain height under the feet are computed exactly from the actual simulator, enabling stable locomotion learning without a critic (value function).

Experiments evaluated these methods on the Unitree G1. Using four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, XMimic learned full-body tracking across all 40 clips of the LAFAN1 dataset in just 0.86 minutes (about 52 seconds), running 3.7 times faster than the prior method BlinkMimic. Furthermore, XSoma cleared the rough-terrain velocity tracking task in 0.77 minutes (about 46 seconds), beating FastSAC—previously the fastest model-free method—by 12.3 times. This demonstrates that world-model-based robot control learning has crossed into an unprecedented sub-minute regime.
contributions: Compiling the entire training loop including MuJoCo Warp with JAX/XLA, eliminating GPU kernel launch overhead almost completely.

Designing an architecture that distributes iterations asynchronously and via pipelining across multiple GPUs for world model training, which previously failed to scale on larger GPUs due to long computational chains.

Achieving fast learning without a critic in locomotion tasks by having the world model predict only robot dynamics, while combining exact geometric calculations (such as terrain height under feet) with straight-through estimation.
Completing motion tracking in 0.86 minutes and rough-terrain locomotion in 0.77 minutes on a Unitree G1—both under one minute of wall-clock time—shattering previous training speed records.

sections.heading: Why world model training stalled on larger GPUs, and what this work aims to fix
sections.summary: While backpropagating analytic gradients through a world model's imagined rollouts is highly sample-efficient for humanoid control, long computational chains prevented it from leveraging faster GPUs. By shortening the training chain, distributing steps across multiple GPUs, and hybridizing the dynamics model with exact geometric calculations, this work learns both motion tracking and rough-terrain locomotion in under a minute.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used to teach humanoid robots how to imitate human motions or walk on rough terrain. While parallel GPU simulation has slashed training times from days down to minutes, methods using world models like SuperMimic have demonstrated even lower computational requirements, thanks to analytic gradients providing vastly lower variance compared to sampling-based gradient estimators like PPO. Recently, implementations like BlinkMimic managed to learn motion tracking on the LAFAN1 dataset in around 3 minutes on a single consumer GPU.

However, existing implementations had a severe bottleneck: upgrading to more powerful GPUs did not make them faster. Running BlinkMimic on an NVIDIA H100 instead of an RTX 4090 yielded almost no speedup. The training loop, including backpropagation through the world model, formed a long chain of countless small, interdependent GPU operations. As a result, execution time was bounded by the sheer number of steps in the computational chain rather than the GPU's raw compute capacity.

Furthermore, progress on rough-terrain locomotion lagged behind. Unlike motion tracking, walking lacks target poses for every step and must account for the terrain underfoot, causing prior world model methods (such as TGI) to take hours. Consequently, the fastest approach remained model-free FastSAC (taking about 15 minutes on a single GPU), leaving world model methods unable to compete in speed.

To solve this, the authors propose "XMimic" and "XSoma," which combine end-to-end compilation in JAX, shortening of the execution chain itself, and distribution across multiple GPUs. With this framework, they aim for sub-minute training times in both motion tracking and rough-terrain locomotion.

sections.heading: Breaking through compute-chain limits with JAX compilation and multi-GPU distribution
sections.summary: Building on BlinkMimic's three-step iteration, the entire training loop is compiled with JAX/MJX and precomputations shorten the chain. XMimic uses pipeline parallelism while XSoma parallelizes successive gradient computations, and XSoma relies on exact terrain calculations to enable critic-free learning with a one-second horizon.
sections.details:
The baseline learning loop comprises three steps: (1) data collection in 4,096 parallel environments, (2) world model updates from the replay buffer, and (3) policy updates through imagined trajectories of $H$ steps inside the world model.

### II-A Compiling the training iteration and shortening the compute chain
XMimic and XSoma write the entire training process—including the physics simulator (MuJoCo Warp with its MJX wrapper)—in JAX, pre-compiling it into an XLA program. Python merely dispatches the program to the GPU and logs results, completely eliminating synchronization waits from Python calls.
In addition, the authors restructured the policy update, which had the longest compute chain. Operations independent of the imagined states (such as observation noise and preprocessing reference motions) were moved outside the rollout, merging and reducing matrix multiplications during backpropagation. Combined with running matrix multiplications in bfloat16 precision, policy update latency was reduced by roughly 40% compared to a direct port.

### II-B Distributing iteration steps across multiple GPUs
Because policy and model parameters change only slightly per iteration, strict completion between steps is unnecessary.
- **XMimic (Pipeline Parallelism)**: Since data collection, model update, and policy update take roughly equal time, each is assigned to a separate GPU (collecting with the policy from one iteration prior, and updating with the model from two iterations prior). A fourth GPU is dedicated exclusively to evaluation resets (identifying failure-prone states and resetting initial conditions), which previously imposed a heavy compute load.
- **XSoma (Concurrent Gradient Computation)**: In velocity tracking, two policy updates are needed for every data collection step, taking about 70% of total iteration time. Here, the first GPU handles collection and model updates, while the remaining three GPUs compute policy gradients concurrently from different batches. By exchanging and applying these gradients sequentially, three policy updates are processed per iteration with tolerable gradient staleness at high speed.

### II-C Extending to rough-terrain locomotion without reference motions (XSoma)
Without target reference motions in locomotion, imagined rollouts drift more easily from real dynamics. XSoma addresses this by leaving only the robot's joint dynamics to the world model, while computing everything geometrically determined—such as foot positions (forward kinematics) and terrain height under the feet (direct lookups from the height field)—exactly from simulator data.
For fall detection, the system checks whether the pelvis or shoulders touch the ground exactly, while using a straight-through estimator with a sigmoid function of clearance during gradient backpropagation. This enables the policy to learn fall avoidance without any critic (value function) over an imagined horizon of just 48 steps (around 1 second at 50 Hz). Furthermore, keeping half of the collection environments deterministic (without action noise) completely prevents policy collapse and falling in the later stages of training.

sections.heading: Proven on four H100s: blistering training speeds and high tracking accuracy
sections.summary: Motion tracking and rough-terrain locomotion were evaluated using the Unitree G1. XMimic tracked all LAFAN1 motions in 0.86 minutes, and XSoma achieved target velocity tracking scores in just 0.77 minutes. Both decisively outperformed existing baselines on a single GPU and widened the lead on multiple GPUs.
sections.details:
All experiments were performed using NVIDIA H100 GPUs within the same cluster. The comparisons focus on wall-clock training time to reach performance thresholds, excluding initial compilation time (20–40 seconds with cache, or about 3 minutes without).

### III-A Motion Tracking (XMimic)
A single policy was trained to track all 40 clips (about 2.5 hours of human motion) from the LAFAN1 dataset using the Unitree G1. The evaluation metric is normalized return (1.0 for perfect tracking), considered complete when maintaining 0.82 or higher across three consecutive evaluations without any falling clips.
- Even on a single GPU, XMimic ran 1.3 times faster than BlinkMimic.
- With four GPUs, iterations per second tripled, easily overcoming a slight increase in required iterations (~10%) due to asynchronous execution.
- As a result, it reached the target in just 0.86 minutes (about 52 seconds), achieving a 3.7x speedup compared to BlinkMimic on a single GPU.

### III-B Rough-Terrain Locomotion (XSoma)
XSoma was compared against FastSAC and PPO on Holosoma's velocity tracking benchmark (flat ground, rough tiles, shallow depressions, randomized mass, friction, and PD gains, with disturbance pushes every 5–10 seconds). The goal was to exceed linear and yaw velocity tracking rewards of 0.95 and 0.80, respectively, across three consecutive runs.
- On a single GPU, XSoma already reached the target in only 1/8 of FastSAC's environment steps and trained in 2.50 minutes, 3.8 times faster than FastSAC.
- On four GPUs, XSoma hit the target in just 0.77 minutes (about 46 seconds). This is 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on a single GPU (~15 minutes). PPO failed to reach the target even after one hour.
- In final tracking accuracy (error between commanded and actual velocity), XSoma had over 30% lower error than FastSAC at 15 minutes of training, highlighting how analytic gradients provide superior walking precision.

sections.heading: Wrap-up and outlook: humanoid reinforcement learning enters the "one-minute" era
sections.summary: By shortening and parallelizing the computational chains that previously bottlenecked GPU processing, this work proves that humanoid motion tracking and locomotion can be learned in under a minute. Future plans include scaling data collection across more GPUs, deploying to real Unitree G1 hardware, and tackling harsher terrains.
sections.details:
This study recognized that the true bottleneck in world-model-based policy learning was not raw GPU compute power, but long dependency chains of small operations, and designed an architecture specifically to eliminate it. By stripping away overhead through JAX compilation and designing task-tailored GPU pipelines, XMimic finishes motion tracking in 0.86 minutes and XSoma finishes rough-terrain locomotion in 0.77 minutes.

With four H100 GPUs, the data collection actor has now become the new primary bottleneck, leading the authors to plan scaling environment step collection across even more GPUs. Additionally, as current validations are purely simulation-based, future work will focus on Sim-to-Real policy deployment onto physical Unitree G1 hardware, as well as extending XSoma to more demanding terrains with larger obstacles and steps.

takeaways: To accelerate world model learning, shortening kernel execution chains and eliminating CPU-GPU / GPU-GPU synchronization overhead is far more critical than raw floating-point compute throughput.
When policy and model changes between iterations are small, asynchronous pipeline parallelism using parameters from 1–2 iterations prior causes virtually no loss in stability or sample efficiency.

For locomotion tasks, delegating only complex dynamics to the world model and hybridizing it with exact geometric computations (like terrain clearance via straight-through estimators) allows stable learning over ultra-short horizons without a critic.
limitations: All experiments were conducted purely in simulation (MuJoCo Warp/MJX); deploying the trained policies onto physical hardware (Unitree G1) and evaluating real-world reality gaps remain future work.

The rough terrain evaluated in the locomotion task consists of tiles and depressions with height variations of only a few centimeters; applicability to more severe, discontinuous terrain such as large stairs or deep gaps remains untested.
While multi-GPU parallelization drastically slashes wall-clock training time, total consumed GPU hours (number of GPUs × time) are slightly higher compared to running on a single GPU.
